On October 12, bulldozers rolled in. The demolition followed expiration of a 24-hour eviction notice issued two days earlier to civilian occupants and traders. For years, the space ahad been a source of discreet income to the Effurun Barracks authorities who allocate space for temporary structures occupied by squatters at negotiated fees and levies But behind the market’s commercial bustle, the authorities said, a darker economy had grown. The eviction which left thousands displaced was carried out to reclaim the land and address pressing security concerns. The real trigger, Vanguard gathered, was a formal complaint to the National Security Adviser in an October 9 letter by the Transmission Company of Nigeria, TCN, signed by its Managing Director/CEO, Dr. Sule Ahmed Abdulaziz. The company said its investigation traced the sabotage to hoodlums operating within and around the Mammy Market on the 3 Battalion grounds along Effurun-Sapele Road. TCN then solicited NSA intervention to direct Brigadier General I B Buhari to take necessary security measures to apprehend and remove the suspects. Abdulaziz wrote: “TCN has been experiencing a series of vandalism targeting its installations around the area of Delta State. These repeated attacks pose a serious threat to the reliability and security of electricity transmission infrastructure in the area. “In the course of our investigation, credible information was gathered indicating that hoodlums operating within and around the Mammy Market are responsible for the attacks and vandalization of TCN installations.” The letter was copied to the Director of Critical National Assets and Infrastructure Protection at the Presidency. The consequential raid ordered by the federal government revealed deeper than anticipated. Fighting one threat exposed another. Though the authorities are shy of talking about it, the military operation reportedly uncovered booming trade in gunrunning, hard drugs and brothels during the demolition. Security sources referenced 40 AK-47 rifles and other ammunition allegedly recovered, with some persons including the market leader reportedly arrested. Brigadier General Ibrahim Baba Buhari, Commander 63 Brigade Asaba and Commander Sector 1, South-South, Operation Delta Safe, was not forthcoming with official position. Neither was the Commanding Officer at the 3 Battalion. But top military sources who spoke behind camera gave insight into the underworld the Effurun Mammy had become. One senior officer explained the procedure for high-profile suspects when Vanguard sought response from relevant military formations in Delta. “If we have caught some people with rifles, that means they are high-profile suspects, right? And, in our mandate, they are not meant to stay with us for a very long time. As soon as we finish our investigation, we hand them over to police, is that so?” He added he was not directly in charge of the market: “I’m just hearing what you’re telling me now. I have to make my own findings also. Me, I’m in the Brigade, not in the sector. And the Mami Market is under the CO 3 Battalion, not under the Brigade or sector.” Another security source who monitored the demolition was more direct about what Mammy harboured: “The location is Uburoko, just right behind the Mami Market. Those are also inside the barracks, that’s where those brothels are, inside the Mammy. “So, that’s where they hide after vandalizing those pylons. So, that people lose electricity, and the national grid is down, it’s because of actions like this.” He said the adjoining scrap market is the real enabler that must be shut: “There’s a need for the scrap market to be scrapped. Otherwise, they are all looting to the scrap market, and the vandalization or vandalism will continue. “Government should close downthat scrap market, because nothing good ever happens out of a scrap market. They call those scrap markets ‘One Naija,’ ‘One Sambisa’. “Once they (stolen power line assets) enter there, under five minutes, they have it dismantled, it’s melted. They harbour them, you can’t separate good people from bad people.” He said vandalism started in December 2025 but became unbearable in August 2026 when 11 pylons were brought down after vandals cut smaller components to weaken the structure. One vandal died when a weakened tower collapsed on him. “That picture of the dead person, he didn’t know the pylon rods had become weak from initial scavenging. So as he was cutting the pipe, the thing just came down on him.” He warned eviction alone will not work because displaced vandals are relocating to a dump site across the road, stressing that police, NDLEA and other agencies find it difficult to enter Mammy because it is taken as a military zone. “The Police, NDLEA and other security agencies, they find it difficult to penetrate and enter (the Mammy) because they take it as a military zone so most of them (vandals) seek safe haven in Mammy.” He defended the operation was not a raid: “We were not even raiding. We were just demolishing. So they are entering, picking their things and leaving. We are not beating anybody, not restricting them.” He said TCN is exhausted by the cost and delay of replacement. “TCN got tired. The one in Delta cannot repair those pylons. They have to get it from outside and it takes months. Just compare the amount of energy being lost to vandals.” Visual evidence shows catastrophic damage – total structural failure of towers like T98 and T100 after systematic stripping of base bracing, angle iron, bolts and gusset plates. TCN’s patrol on Delta/Afisere 132kV line found nine towers – T9, T10, T11, T12, T14, T15, T16, T17 & T18 – vandalised and needing urgent rehabilitation to avoid collapse. Not An Isolated Case The pattern is not limited to Delta. In Rivers State, advocate Alhaji Brian Barile who documents vandalism from Afam Power Plant, Oyigbo to Elelenwon in Obio/Akpor said: “From Elelenwon to Oyigbo, all the base braces and components of the electricity towers are gone, all stolen.” He described what he met around Green City Estate: “I was on the railway from Elelewon to Ogba side doing some work when I decided to stroll within Elelewon, under the Green City Estate, around the designated International Cattle Market when I discovered the mind-boggling vandalism.” Comparing untouched and vandalised towers, he said, “I saw one (pylon) untouched because there are living houses surrounding. You can see it’s complete, untouched, formidable and giving the pylon strength to stand.” “Others have been compromised, vandalised. They’ve everything at the base removed and you can see the pole (mast) bending. Anything can happen now. The strength of these poles are gone.” For TCN, the bulldozers in Mammy were not just about land. It was a desperate push to save the national grid from a dark economy of scrap, arms and drugs thriving behind barracks gates. For the law-abiding among thousands of squatters evicted from the Mammy, the bulldozers also left in their trail huge human cost in loss of property and livelihoods many would take who knows how long to recover from. The respected Eze Ihenetu had organised a congregation of Igbo and Ghanaian leaders for a traditional cocktail reception. According to the major propeller of the project Kelvin King Dawie of King Dawie Publishing Ltd (KPL) “When people ask why Pete Edochie, I tell them that no honor for Pete Edochie is too big. He has very much distinguished himself on the continent of Africa and beyond as a custodian of the cultural heritage of Africa and has been consistent in it for decades since mounting the stage at the tender age of 15. He is well known and received a lot of honors and awards globally including Nigeria’s national honor of merit; MON. “We also looked at the way he has distinguished himself on stage and in communication which has warranted him receiving Honorary Doctorate in Literature and creative arts. It also reveals that Nigeria and Ghana have co-existed as West Africa’s beloved Anglophone countries despite hiccups occasioned by various ‘Ghana must go’ or ‘Nigeria must go’ agitations. And to see both Nigerians and Ghanaians under one roof because of Pete Edochie, animosities may have been doused even if for a moment. The unveiling of the autobiographical book; Titan of Africa, the story of Pete Edochie, published by KPL Publishers was a big attraction on its own and first of its kind for a Nigerian actor. The event which held at Kempiski Accra drew together distinguished Ghanaians with highlights including his meeting with Ghanaian legendary actress, broadcaster and musician Grace Omaboe, known to many as Maame Dokono. item.title: From Atiku’s spokesmen to Tinubu’s spokesmen – yesterday, Atiku; today, Tinubu; tomorrow, who knows?, by Stephanie Shaakaa
item.description: A microphone has no permanent owner. The man holding it today may well be holding it for somebody else tomorrow. Segun Showunmi has given Nigerians another reason to examine the curious business of political loyalty. Read Also: 2027: Atiku suffering from ‘Emir complex’ — Segun Sowunmi On October 15, 2026, he urged the public to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, declaring that prosperity is around the corner. He is now part of Tinubu’s presidential campaign communications team, persuading citizens that the President deserves four more years. There is a detail worth remembering. Showunmi was the spokesman for Atiku Abubakar’s presidential campaign in 2019. Daniel Bwala, who served as a spokesman for Atiku’s 2023 campaign, is now Tinubu’s Special Adviser on Media and Public Communication. If Nigerian politics were a church, these two would have explaining to do about their conversion. One can almost see the congregation watching as yesterday’s defenders of one ambition arrive to preach the merits of another. The faces are familiar. The voices have not changed. Only the object of their praise has. Showunmi and Bwala are free to change their minds. Nobody owns another man’s political allegiance forever. They can leave a party, embrace a former opponent, and discover fresh reasons to support a politician they once challenged. That is their constitutional right. But there is a vast difference between changing your mind and expecting the public to develop amnesia. These men were not casual supporters arguing politics over drinks. They were campaign spokesmen. They stood before cameras, spoke to journalists, defended their principals, and tried to persuade Nigerians to see presidential candidates through a specific lens. Their words were meant to shape public opinion in a contest for the highest office in the land. When Daniel Bwala declared on social media before his crossover that “The human brain is unique and miraculous… UNTIL YOU JOIN APC, THEN IT STOPS WORKING,” he was not offering a lighthearted joke. He was selling Nigerians a definitive moral assessment. Yet after joining the President’s camp, he brushed aside his past critiques during an Al Jazeera interview by insisting, “It’s all politics.” Really? If a spokesman can spend an election campaign arguing that a candidate is a threat to the nation, then cross over to that candidate’s camp and declare his former denunciations irrelevant, where does campaign duty end and personal conviction begin? Now the scenery has changed, and the public is expected to receive their new message with the same confidence with which they delivered the old one. Showunmi’s declaration that prosperity is around the corner makes the issue particularly urgent. Nigerians have spent years hearing explanations for hardship, assurances that reforms will eventually pay off, and promises that the pain of today is the price of a better tomorrow. But there is a vast difference between changing your mind and expecting the public to develop amnesia. These men were not casual supporters arguing politics over drinks. They were campaign spokesmen. They stood before cameras, spoke to journalists, defended their principals, and tried to persuade Nigerians to see presidential candidates through a specific lens. Their words were meant to shape public opinion in a contest for the highest office in the land. When Daniel Bwala declared on social media before his crossover that “The human brain is unique and miraculous… UNTIL YOU JOIN APC, THEN IT STOPS WORKING,” he was not offering a lighthearted joke. He was selling Nigerians a definitive moral assessment. Yet after joining the President’s camp, he brushed aside his past critiques during an Al Jazeera interview by insisting, “It’s all politics.” Really? If a spokesman can spend an election campaign arguing that a candidate is a threat to the nation, then cross over to that candidate’s camp and declare his former denunciations irrelevant, where does campaign duty end and personal conviction begin? Now the scenery has changed, and the public is expected to receive their new message with the same confidence with which they delivered the old one. Showunmi’s declaration that prosperity is around the corner makes the issue particularly urgent. Nigerians have spent years hearing explanations for hardship, assurances that reforms will eventually pay off, and promises that the pain of today is the price of a better tomorrow. The market woman still calculates what she can afford before buying food. The worker still watches transport fares swallow a growing share of his salary. Parents still struggle with school fees, rent, electricity bills, and the cost of keeping a household running. For millions of people, the corner called prosperity has become a destination repeatedly announced but never quite reached. Showunmi is entitled to believe Tinubu deserves another term. But he must do more than announce that better days are approaching. He should tell Nigerians what evidence supports his optimism, what tangible improvements they should already see, and when the promised relief will begin to make a difference in their lives. A campaign spokesman can sell hope; he cannot demand that hardship be mistaken for progress simply because he has found a more powerful principal. If Tinubu’s reforms are working, Showunmi should make the case. If the President’s policies have put Nigeria on a path to growth, let him explain the evidence and show how the benefits will reach ordinary households. If continuity is the answer, let him explain why citizens should endure another four years rather than choose a different direction. The microphone gives him an audience. It does not give him immunity from questions. Perhaps Bwala sincerely reconsidered his position. Perhaps Showunmi discovered genuine merit in the President’s leadership. People can change their minds for valid reasons, and we need not invent sinister motives to demand an explanation. The metaphor that clings most obstinately to this political culture remains transactional,an indictment of an establishment where political conviction lasts only as long as the arrangement remains lucrative. Welcome to the Nigerian political marketplace, where the occupants change rooms, the promises acquire fresh packaging, and yesterday’s sworn enemies discover they have always shared common ground. The cost of this arrangement is not merely the embarrassment of watching familiar faces defend unfamiliar positions. It is the steady erosion of public trust. When political arguments change with the fortunes of the people making them, citizens have reason to question whether they are hearing honest assessments of the country’s problems or simply the latest sales pitch from a campaign office. Showunmi and Bwala need not apologize for leaving Atiku’s camp. They do, however, have an opportunity to demonstrate that their present positions rest on more than the convenience of political realignment. They can explain what they believe Tinubu has done right, address what he has done wrong, and make a credible case for why another term would serve Nigeria’s interests. As 2027 approaches, the country will be crowded with people eager to explain why their preferred candidate deserves power. Some will have remained loyal to one camp for decades. Others will have traveled through several parties, alliances, and campaign offices. Voters should judge each argument on its merits, but they must not be expected to forget the history of the people making it. Nigerians are not an audience to be entertained between elections, nor are they customers obliged to buy whatever a familiar salesman places before them. They have to live with the consequences of political decisions long after campaign slogans have faded and spokesmen have moved on. Showunmi can tell Nigerians that prosperity is near. Bwala can defend the President’s record. Both men can campaign for Tinubu with all the eloquence they possess. But the public is entitled to place their present arguments beside their past ones and ask the question that neither a new title nor a new political uniform can make disappear. If you were right then, what changed? And if you are right now, why should we believe you? Asking these questions is not persecution,it is the tax every holder of a public microphone must pay. Holding men to their own recorded words is not an attack,it is the bare minimum duty of a critical electorate. The microphone may belong to whoever is holding it. The judgment belongs to the people listening. For the Registry, the most neglected but most dangerous, total digitalization is needed: electronic filing with time stamps, CCTV in registries, and audit trails will end the era where a clerk can decide the fate of a governorship. Above all, speed is essential. The 180-day rule for tribunals must be sacrosanct, because the longer a petition stays in the system, the more time for market-stall bargaining. Justice Augie has sounded the alarm, and the CJN, NBA, EFCC, ICPC, and civil society must act now. If we lose the courts before February 2027, we would have lost the election before the first vote is cast.” Courtroom should not be turned into final polling unit where money casts deciding vote — Adewale On his part, former SDP chairman in Ondo state, Hon Stephen Adewale said, “Justice Augie’s warning should trouble every Nigerian as we approach the 2027 elections. If politicians believe they can purchase judicial protection, electoral malpractice becomes a calculated investment. A stolen mandate could pass through the courts and emerge wearing the robes of legitimacy. Corruption among registry officials can be equally destructive, especially where evidence is concealed or access to documents is deliberately frustrated. The damage could outlive the election. Clean up judiciary to save Nigeria’s democracy — Ambakaderimo For Elder Joseph Ambakederimo, Convener South South Reawakening Group, “The retired Supreme Court Justice tried to be lenient on her colleagues at the Bench, Bar, and the Registry. Ekwueme understood that the survival of Nigeria as a united nation depended, to a considerable extent, on addressing the fears of domination, exclusion, and marginalisation among its constituent ethnic and regional groups. THE QUEST FOR NATIONAL INTEGRATION Following the end of the Nigerian Civil War in 1970, the urgent questions of national reconstruction, reconciliation, and the restoration of confidence among the country’s diverse peoples occupied a central place in political discourse. These concerns became particularly prominent during the formation of political parties in 1978, as Nigeria prepared for a return to civilian rule. The political parties recognised, to varying degrees, the need to accommodate the country’s complex ethnic and regional composition. The National Party of Nigeria (NPN), which eventually won the presidential election, adopted a political arrangement that reflected the importance of balancing interests across the North and the South in the distribution of key political offices. It was within this political atmosphere that Dr. Alex Ekwueme emerged as the NPN’s vice-presidential candidate, alongside Alhaji Shehu Shagari as its presidential candidate. The significance of the Igbo presence in the vice-presidential calculations of the major political parties of the period deserves particular attention. With the exception of the Nigerian People’s Party (NPP), whose presidential candidate, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, chose Professor Ishaya Audu as his running mate, the other major parties also featured Igbo politicians as their vice-presidential candidates. These choices were politically significant. At the very least, they reflected an awareness of the need to broaden the political coalitions upon which the Nigerian federation rested and to reassure the Igbo people that, despite the devastation of the Civil War, they remained an integral part of the Nigerian project. It would, however, be a mistake to regard these political arrangements as merely symbolic. They raised a fundamental question about the future of Nigeria: could the country achieve genuine reconciliation and lasting unity without creating a political environment in which every major ethnic and regional group had a fair opportunity to participate in national leadership? The prospect of an Igbo man ascending to the presidency subsequently became a subject of considerable political sensitivity. It has been suggested that apprehensions about Dr. Ekwueme’s possible emergence as President, particularly in the context of political succession under the Shagari administration, formed part of the considerations surrounding the military coup of December 1983. While such claims require careful examination against the available historical record, they underscore a larger and more enduring problem: the difficulty Nigeria has faced in separating the legitimate pursuit of political power from fears about the ethnic or regional identity of those who might exercise it. The lesson is unmistakable. National unity cannot be sustained by rhetoric alone. It requires deliberate political arrangements, mutual trust, and a willingness to accommodate the legitimate aspirations of all sections of the country. FROM MILITARY RULE TO THE QUEST FOR A NEW NIGERIA The military coup that terminated the Second Republic in December 1983 abruptly ended the democratic experiment in which Dr. Ekwueme had played such a prominent role. He was subsequently detained by the military authorities and subjected to imprisonment. Yet, in a remarkable demonstration of intellectual resilience, that period of confinement provided him with an opportunity to reflect more deeply on the Nigerian condition and to nurture his ideas about the kind of country Nigeria ought to become. Rather than seize the opportunity to address the structural problems that had contributed to political instability, mutual suspicion, and the struggle for power, successive military administrations introduced institutional changes that, in my view, further complicated Nigeria’s national question. The creation of additional states and local government areas, the delineation of electoral constituencies, and the conduct and interpretation of population censuses became contentious issues in the struggle over political representation and the distribution of national resources. The consequences were particularly troubling for what is today the South-East geopolitical zone, whose concerns about representation and its relative position within the federation have remained important elements of the national debate. The point is not that every administrative or political change undertaken under military rule was necessarily designed to disadvantage a particular region. Rather, it is that institutional arrangements introduced without sufficient regard for fairness, transparency, and the confidence of all constituent groups can deepen existing grievances and undermine national cohesion. The failure of the Babangida administration to complete a credible transition to democratic rule, culminating in the annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, further aggravated the national crisis and deepened public distrust of the political process. It was against this background of political uncertainty, institutional distrust, and unresolved questions of national identity that Dr. Ekwueme, having endured detention and imprisonment, began to engage more actively with like-minded Nigerians on the need to reconstruct the Nigerian federation on a more equitable foundation. INEC must scrutinise the names it receives, verify identities and supervise workers on election day. Political parties and their agents, meanwhile, have a role in observing the process and raising concerns through proper channels. Igini said INEC’s senior officials would not be present at every polling unit on election day. The work would be carried out by temporary staff under the commission’s supervision, making the quality of that supervision central to the process. item.title: Ebola Vaccine Trial Begins In DR Congo – WHO Chief
item.description: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said. The DR Congo’s worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600. Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic. A health official works in the laboratory extraction room of the Institute of Lassa Fever Research and Control in Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital in Irrua, Edo State, midwest Nigeria, on March 6, 2018. Photo by PIUS UTOMI EKPEI / AFP Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo. “Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia, DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means ‘hope’ in Swahili,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X. “This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work. “In the meantime, the existing Everbo vaccine (licensed for use in preventing other Ebola virus disease) will be tested. “WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives.” The so-called Tumaini trial in the DRC — a single trial framework that can test the safety and efficacy of multiple vaccines — should also eventually incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are moving through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials. One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology. item.title: Enugu Rangers Crash Out Of CAF Champions League After Late Collapse To MC Alger
item.description: Nigerian champions Rangers International of Enugu crashed out of the CAF Champions League on Friday after losing 3-0 to Algeria’s MC Alger at the Ali La Pointe Stadium in Algiers. The defeat handed Rangers a 3-2 aggregate loss, despite their 2-0 victory over the Algerians in the first leg in Abeokuta last weekend. The Flying Antelopes failed to protect their advantage, succumbing to late pressure as MC Alger scored three unanswered goals to secure a place in the group stage. After a goalless first half, MC Alger needed three goals in the remaining 45 minutes to overturn the deficit and keep their campaign alive. Enugu Rangers defender tries to stop MC Alger attacker in CAF Champions League game in Algiers on Friday, October 23, 2026. Photo Credit: CAF Online The comeback began in the 58th minute when Chahreddine Boukholda put the hosts ahead, raising hopes among their supporters. With six minutes left in regulation time, Guinean forward Mohamed Bangoura scored MC Alger’s second goal to level the tie at 2-2 on aggregate, sparking celebrations in the stands. As the match appeared to be heading for a penalty shootout, Soufiane Bayazid struck three minutes into stoppage time to complete MC Alger’s comeback and seal a 3-0 win on the night and a 3-2 aggregate victory. The result ended Rangers’ bid to reach the group stage, while MC Alger will now seek to advance further in the competition as they pursue a second continental title, 50 years after winning it in 1976. item.title: Trump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms
item.description: President Donald Trump’s administration lifted some tariffs on Canadian imports Friday, two weeks ahead of midterm elections, after a vulnerable Republican candidate said she’d lobbied for the change. The easing of tariffs will apply to products including “plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment,” the White House said in a statement. The change could help Senator Susan Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democrat in the US-Canada border state of Maine, which has been hit hard by Trump’s trade war. She posted on social media that she had “secured” the exemptions for “products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.” Democrats are targeting Collins’s seat in their attempt to win control of Congress from the Republicans in the November 3 midterms. The economies of the United States and Canada are heavily inter-connected, with roughly 70 percent of all Canadian exports heading to the United States. Tensions between the North American neighbors have been high since trade talks broke down in August, with Trump imposing a slew of new tariffs in response. Friday’s action lifts tariffs on certain goods, but imposes levies on new ones, including carpets, certain valves and waste products, the White House said. The new measures will take effect on October 30. Collins said many farmers in her state “rely on specialized equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.” Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminum and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth. Canada has entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction. Trump’s tariffs enforced after the talks broke down impacted around $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement. Since taking power in his second term, Trump has upended the global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on friend and foe alike, saying that other countries have been taking advantage of the United States. He has also explicitly tied some threatened tariffs to political or foreign policy objectives. The post Trump lifts some Canada tariffs ahead of midterms appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Nigeria’s first Ebola case ‘highly similar’ to Kenyan one – Minister
item.description: Genomic tests have shown that the Ebola virus found in Nigeria’s first case resembles that of the first case recorded in Kenya earlier this month, Nigeria’s health minister said Friday. Nigeria announced its first Ebola case on Tuesday, the wife of a staff member at Switzerland’s embassy in Abuja, who had returned from Uganda on October 3. She had not visited the Democratic Republic of Congo — the epicentre of the current outbreak, the Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday, contrary to earlier reports by the Ugandan government. Health authorities on the continent have been trying to trace the source of her infection — with Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention earlier suggesting she may have come into contact at the airport with Kenya’s first patient, who also flew from Uganda on the same day. Based on the the genomic analysis, the case in Nigeria “appears to be closely related to the case identified in the index case in Kenya”, Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told reporters. “There is no evidence of travel of that index case in Kenya that links it to Nigeria, but the viruses are appearing to be related,” he said, adding in a post on X that the case “is highly similar to that from Kenya”. Following the DRC, Uganda and Kenya, Nigeria has become the fourth African country to be affected by the Bundibugyo species outbreak. After flaring up in the northeastern DRC in May, the deadly viral haemorrhagic fever spread into neighbouring Uganda, where 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths were recorded before the outbreak there was officially over in August. To date, the epidemic has surpassed 9,700 confirmed cases, including 4,690 deaths, according to WHO figures as of October 20. item.title: Nigeria’s Power Minister Commissions 120MVA Transmission Substation In Katsina
item.description: Katsina State has recorded another major milestone in its quest for improved electricity supply as the Minister of Power, Joseph Olasunkanmi Tegbe, and Governor Dikko Umaru Radda commissioned the newly completed 120 MVA, 132/33 kV Transmission Substation in Kankia Local Government Area. Speaking at the commissioning ceremony on Friday, the Minister described the project as a key component of the Federal Government’s strategic efforts to strengthen Nigeria’s national grid and expand electricity transmission capacity across the country. He reaffirmed President Bola Tinubu’s administration’s commitment to delivering critical power infrastructure that will ensure electricity generated across the country is efficiently transmitted to homes, businesses and industries. Governor Dikko Radda hailed the completion of the substation as a landmark investment in Katsina’s power infrastructure, noting that the facility, equipped with two 60MVA transformers with a combined capacity of 120MVA, will significantly reinforce the state’s transmission network and enable greater volumes of electricity to reach consumers. Radda stressed that reliable electricity remains the backbone of economic growth, industrialisation and improved public service delivery, adding that the project will complement Katsina’s expanding renewable energy programme while boosting key sectors such as agriculture, agro-processing, commerce, education and healthcare. Governor Radda expressed appreciation to President Tinubu for approving the project and commended the Minister of Power and the Transmission Company of Nigeria for ensuring its successful completion. He also urged residents of the host community to safeguard the facility against vandalism, describing it as a strategic national asset that will serve present and future generations. item.title: INEC Legally Bound To Publish Voters’ Register Online – Itodo
item.description: The Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, says the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) is legally required to publish the voters’ register online ahead of the 2027 general elections. Itodo’s position follows calls by opposition politicians and civil society groups for the electoral body to make the register available online. Speaking on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday, he said the demand was backed by Section 19 of the Electoral Act 2026, which provides for the publication of the register both at designated physical locations and online. “I think on this point about the release of the voters’ register, the law is very clear in Section 19 of the 2026 Electoral Act that after voter registration, there is claims and objections and that claims and objections shall happen not later that 90 days, in other words, it can happen earlier than 90 days but not later than 90 days before the day of an election. And what will be the mode? First, you publish in your offices or across the polling units and on INEC website or any website officially designated by INEC,” Itodo said. ﻿ He said INEC had indicated that the claims and objections exercise had been conducted across the country through physical visits to designated locations. However, he noted that the voters’ register was still unavailable on the commission’s website or any other officially designated website. “What INEC has said is that the claims and objections has been conducted across the country and what you might call manually or the one that requires physical visitation of those areas but the one online as of today, the voters’ register is not on INEC’s website or on any official website. And what the law says in Section 19 of the Act is INEC shall, which means it is compulsory,” he said. Itodo maintained that INEC was required to publish the register online in addition to displaying it at polling units, adding that the commission had failed to comply with that provision 85 days before the election. He urged the electoral body to explain why it had not published the register online, warning that its silence could undermine public confidence. “I think INEC owes it to the Nigerian voters to really make a statement as to why it has not been able to implement this part of the law. This silence does not inspire confidence, so INEC needs to explain to the people. In so far as you haven’t explained to the people and there is silence, it raises a lot of questions,” Itodo added. item.title: Fubara Promises 700 Shops At Creek Road Market By January 2027
item.description: The Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, says the first phase of the Creek Road Market reconstruction in Old Port Harcourt Township will provide about 700 shops for traders, ease traffic congestion, and improve trading conditions. Governor Fubara stated this during an inspection of the ongoing project, where he expressed satisfaction with the quality and progress of work. He said the new market would accommodate wet and dry goods traders, particularly women currently selling along Creek Road and adjoining streets, allowing for the rehabilitation of surrounding roads. “With 700 shops, it is clear that our women who are trading along the Creek Road will be relocated, and we’ll have freer access along the road,” the Governor said. Fubara described Old Port Harcourt Township as a historic part of the city, home to elderly residents and the original inhabitants, whom he referred to as the “Aborigines.” Governor Siminalayi Fubara of Rivers State (centre). He stressed the need to restore the area’s cleanliness and dignity, noting that street trading had extended beyond Creek Road to other roads in the township. “It’s important we tidy up this road so that these traders can evacuate the major road, and the road will be free,” he said. The Governor assured that his administration would provide the necessary support to ensure the project’s timely completion, adding that the contractor had promised delivery by the end of January 2027. The project forms part of the Fubara administration’s urban renewal efforts to improve commercial activities, ease traffic movement and create a cleaner environment in Port Harcourt. item.title: Zamfara Govt Deploys Medical Personnel To Airport, Motor Parks For Ebola Screening
item.description: The Zamfara State Government has deployed medical personnel to Gusau International Airport and major motor parks across the state to screen passengers and strengthen surveillance against the spread of Ebola Virus Disease. Zamfara State Commissioner for Health, Nafisa Maradun, disclosed this while leading a medical team to flag off the screening of passengers arriving at the Gusau International Airport. Nafisa said medical personnel had also been deployed to major motor parks across the state to ensure early detection and prompt reporting of suspected cases. She noted that the screening exercise had identified a passenger with an elevated body temperature who arrived in Gusau after returning from Saudi Arabia. The state government has also directed public and private health facilities, disease surveillance officers and local government health authorities to strengthen preparedness and response measures against the disease. The Director of Public Health Services, Yusuf Abubakar, issued the directive on behalf of the Commissioner for Health during a meeting with health stakeholders and representatives of the Nigeria Customs Service, Nigeria Immigration Service and the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW). Abubakar said the Customs and Immigration Services would support surveillance at border entry points, while the NURTW would assist in monitoring passengers at motor parks and alerting relevant authorities to suspected cases. He directed disease surveillance officers across the state’s 14 local government areas to notify health facilities, intensify routine and event-based surveillance, and ensure the prompt reporting of suspected cases. The Director also disclosed that the ministry had commenced temperature screening, sensitisation of frontline health workers, identification of passengers of interest and activation of response mechanisms at different levels. He further directed health facilities to strengthen screening and triage procedures, infection prevention and control, early identification of suspected cases, immediate notification and safe referral. The State Epidemiology Unit and relevant public health authorities are also expected to assess the state’s preparedness, including isolation facilities, referral arrangements, trained personnel, personal protective equipment, laboratory procedures and emergency logistics. The ministry called on relevant stakeholders to work together to strengthen surveillance and ensure strict compliance with public health guidelines to protect residents of Zamfara State and prevent the spread of the disease.
